title: Hearth and the Stubborn Ram
markdown:
Way up high, where the clouds tickle the tallest peaks, a chain of mountains is joined by ropes as strong as dragon whiskers. It is wild and wonderful: soaring birds, puffing clouds, Sky-Folk banners that whip like laundry in a hurry. On one of the sturdiest peaks, in a sturdy stone cottage, lives an ogre named Hearth, not a grumpy ogre but warm as a hearth fire, twinkling-eyed, rumbling-gentle, hands as soft as moss.

Hearth’s unusual pet is Beryl, a mountain ram of fluffy white curls like spun moonlight, hooves sure as stone, heart stout as any goat’s. When Beryl thinks a thing is important, those hooves plant as if they have grown roots.

Not stubborn. Keeping safe.

One blustery morning the wind howls like a hungry wolf. The Sky-Folk’s ferry rope needs securing across a big gap. Hearth’s job is simple: keep Beryl out of the way. At the very moment the grand ferry needs to swing, Beryl plants. Plants as if they have become part of the mountain.

“Oh, botheration and puff,” puffs Zephyr, a wispy Sky-Folk elder with a nose always pink from weather. “That ram. Always at the worst moment.” Her plan is neat and not very clever. “We’ll just push the ram.” Other Sky-Folk flutter down and heave at woolly sides. Beryl braces, horns pointed bravely skyward.

Hearth watches from a safe distance. On one large shoulder sits Fidget, a goblin of twitching pointy ears and bright darting eyes. “That neatest-looking plan,” Hearth rumbles, a chuckle like stones on a gentle slope, “isn’t the cleverest at all.”

Fidget can spot a worry from a mile of mist. While the Sky-Folk huff and nearly fall off the mountain, he notices Beryl’s ears. Not the ears of a creature being difficult. “It’s not just stubbornness. Beryl thinks the rope might slip. Protecting us, in their own way.”

“Keeping safe by becoming a woolly boulder?” Hearth looks from ram to swirling mist. A narrow cave mouth waits a short climb away. For a moment a faint shimmer shows inside, like a captured star.

“We cannot possibly panic yet. We have not even had our mid-morning tea.” Hearth takes a thermos from their belt, pours fragrant chamomile into two strong mugs, and sits on a mossy rock, not too close to Beryl, not too far to be ignored. Steam leans toward the ram.

“Just a moment, old friend. The wind is frisky. A good cup of tea helps you think clearly.”

Slurping. Warmth. Hearth’s steady presence. Beryl’s stiff ears un-prick a fraction. Hearth points a large green finger at a small pool by the cave. The sun finds a gap in the cloud. The cave mouth, which had looked merely dark, throws gold into the water. Treasure-light. Sparkle and dance.

Beryl’s duty-fixed eyes widen. The planted hooves remember they can walk. One tentative step. Another. The ferry rope is forgotten. The ram ambles toward the pool, drawn by that captivating shine.

The Sky-Folk gasp, then cheer. “Remarkable,” cries Zephyr, pink nose wiggling. “Our way of doing things worked. We showed Beryl who was boss.”

Hearth smiles, slow, eyes crinkling, and pats a woolly flank. Fidget examines a particularly interesting pebble and winks.

Later the rope is secured. The wind sighs through the passes as if it, too, has had tea. Hearth sits with Beryl and offers plump dried mountain berries, Beryl’s favourite. The ram nudges Hearth’s hand, a soft nuzzle, no speech required. Chamomile steam still lifts from the second mug. Gold light ticks in the pool. Hooves rest, unplanted, in wet shining stone.

Not stubborn. Keeping safe. The ferry swings, empty of rams, and the mountain keeps its quiet.
characters: Hearth (warm ogre), Fidget (a goblin of great wit)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain adventure fantasy for ages 9-10
author: StoryGen Community
